items.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Ella Fitzgerald always closed the show, which she should. Who’s going to follow that? She was great. Playing for her, we took turns.

ctx.x: Fabulous. It was in every language a highlight. All the guys played well. I played – the drummers were Buddy Rich and myself. Ella Fitzgerald always closed the show, which she should. Who’s going to follow that? She was great. Playing for her, we took turns. I’d play the first half. Then Buddy would play the first half the second part of the tour. The first part was, all the instruments played. The second part was always the guest artists, like Lionel Hampton, Buddy DeFranco, and Oscar and Ray Brown. A lot of…
When you have a group of musicians like that who come from so many different styles, what was that like to be the drummer and to be responsive to all those different types of approaches?

items.title: Louie Bellson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996
items.q: Ella Fitzgerald would come on the show, Joe Williams, Tony Bennett, Duke, whoever it was, Dizzy.

ctx.x: Joe Williams? Absolutely. There is an example, well he’s such a great talent, but what makes Joe Williams so great, is not only is he one of the greatest singers in the world, but when he comes in to rehearse, he comes in like a gentleman, he knows exactly what he wants to rehearse, what he wants to work out, he does it, he’s in and out with no problems. That to me is a real artist you know? Because he knows exactly what the band should sound like, what the dynamic should be, what he wants from the drummer, and…

never had trouble with the biggies. Ella Fitzgerald would come on the show, Joe Williams, Tony Bennett, Duke, whoever it was, Dizzy. In and out. It was always that person that didn’t quite make it that — “something is wrong with the dressing room.”
